title: Royce White, Etan Thomas Clash Over Kyrie and Kaepernick
htmlContent:
Royce White is no stranger to stirring the pot, and his latest take turned an Instagram comment section into a debate about activism, honesty, and the responsibility that comes with an athlete's platform.

Brandon "Scoop B" Robinson shared a clip on Instagram from his recent interview with White, the former NBA first-round pick and 2024 Republican U.S. Senate nominee in Minnesota. In it, White made a comparison guaranteed to spark a reaction.

"Kyrie Irving has surpassed Colin Kaepernick in terms of the genuine impact of his public platform," White said.
View this post on Instagram

A post shared by 👑Brandon “Scoop B” Robinson (@scoopb)

Robinson framed the clip around the shift in athlete platforms and cultural influence, writing that White "didn't hold back." The comment section quickly proved him right.

Etan Thomas, the former NBA forward who played for the Washington Wizards, Oklahoma City Thunder and Atlanta Hawks and has since built a career as an author and activist, was among the first to respond.

"It's not a competition," Thomas wrote.

White's reply was short and pointed.

"Are you vaccinated?" he asked Thomas.

The question was a clear nod to one of the defining moments of Irving's career. In 2021, Irving refused to get the COVID-19 vaccine, which kept him off the court for much of the Brooklyn Nets' season under New York City's vaccine mandate. Supporters praised him for standing firm at great professional cost, while critics called it a distraction. White's question suggested that, for him, Irving's willingness to sacrifice games and money is part of what makes his platform authentic.

About an hour later, Bronx rapper and activist Mysonne Linen joined the conversation, siding with Thomas on the bigger picture while calling for unity.

"I agree, but this is what we create when we are divided!" Linen wrote. "Had someone posted this comparison to Jay-Z you would've either agreed or not commented based on your perspective and belief. Instead of us acknowledging the good our people do we point out their flaws and discrediting them. Love bro."

White did not budge.

"Division is a natural consequence of dishonesty," he replied to Linen.

Linen, a co-founder of the social justice organization Until Freedom, answered with a philosophical response of his own.

"Your perception is your reality beloved; everyone has a different perspective and rendition," he wrote.

White pushed back again, rejecting the idea that truth depends on perspective.

"No, there is 1 universal truth," White wrote. "We know the truth… We avoid it because the benefits of bulls--- are too good."

As of this writing, Linen had the latest word in the exchange.

"There's not always a universal truth because everyone's reality is different," he wrote.

The back-and-forth captured a debate that has followed athlete activism for years: is impact measured by visibility, by sacrifice, or by results?

Kaepernick's case is well documented. He first sat, then knelt, during the national anthem in the 2016 preseason to protest police brutality and racial injustice. He has not played in the NFL since that season. He later settled a collusion grievance with the league in 2019 and launched the Know Your Rights Camp, a youth empowerment organization. For many, his protest remains the defining act of modern athlete activism because of what it cost him.

Irving's influence has taken a different shape. Beyond his stance on vaccines, he has spoken openly about his Native American heritage and his connection to the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe. During the 2020 WNBA season, he committed $1.5 million to help supplement the salaries of players who chose not to play in the league's bubble. He has also been at the center of controversy that critics say complicates any claim about his platform's greater impact.

It is not the first time White has aimed at Kaepernick. In the same interview with Robinson, he questioned why Kaepernick is still a fixture in mainstream media and challenged him to "evolve" his protest to new institutions.

White, one of the first NBA players to publicly push for mental health accommodations after Houston drafted him 16th overall in 2012, has built his post-basketball identity on saying what others will not.

For now, the debate White started is far from settled, and judging by the comment section, neither side is ready to log off.
excerpt: Royce White's claim that Kyrie Irving has surpassed Colin Kaepernick in genuine platform impact ignited a spirited Instagram debate with former NBA forward and activist Etan Thomas, rapper Mysonne Linen, and others over what athlete activism truly means and costs.
